subtypes.name: 2D area or perimeter: plug in and combine
subtypes.tell: You get a rectangle, square or triangle, either drawn or described with its dimensions, and the question asks for its area or perimeter. The question may also ask for the total of two shapes, or what is left when one shape is cut out of another. Some choices are expressions in a variable, and one of them is usually the perimeter when the question asks for area, or the other way round.
subtypes.method: 1) Check whether the question asks for area (square units) or perimeter (units). 2) Write the formula: A = lw, A = s², A = ½bh, or perimeter = the sum of all sides. For a right triangle, the base and height are the two legs, so leave out the longest side. 3) Substitute the numbers. Add the areas for a combined figure, and subtract for a cut-out.
subtypes.desmos: Useful for arithmetic only. Type ½·b·h or the sum of the sides to check your number. It does not help you choose the right formula.
subtypes.trap: The wrong choices are perimeter-for-area swaps, the base alone without the ½, and triangle areas that use the hypotenuse as the height. For an equilateral triangle, you may multiply one side by 4 as if it were a square.

subtypes.name: Volume of a named solid
subtypes.tell: The question names a solid (rectangular prism, cylinder, cone, pyramid, sphere or hemisphere) and gives its dimensions, sometimes on a labelled figure. It asks for the volume. Choices often leave π in the answer, or the question asks for the value next to π.
subtypes.method: 1) Look up the formula on the reference sheet. Cones and pyramids get ⅓, a sphere is (4/3)πr³, and a hemisphere is half of that. 2) Before substituting, turn a diameter into a radius and apply any percent change to the dimension. 3) Substitute and simplify, leaving π in if the choices keep it.
subtypes.desmos: Type the formula with the numbers substituted, for example (1/3)π r² h with r and h filled in, and compare the result to the choices. If the choices have π in them, divide your result by π.
subtypes.trap: The question gives you a diameter so that you will use it as the radius, which makes the answer 4 times too big. You may also forget the ⅓ for a cone or pyramid, or the ½ for a hemisphere. When a dimension is scaled by a percent, you may apply the percent to the volume instead of to the radius.

subtypes.name: Given the area or volume, find a dimension
subtypes.tell: The area or volume is already given as a number, and the question asks for a missing length: a base, an edge, a radius or a labelled variable on a figure. The answer is a length.
subtypes.method: 1) Write the formula and set it equal to the given area or volume. 2) Substitute every dimension you know. 3) Isolate the unknown: divide, then take a square root if the unknown is squared, and keep only the positive root.
subtypes.desmos: This is very useful. Type the formula as an equation in x, for example (1/3)π(3)² x = 473 or 8x² = 1152, and read off the x-intercept or intersection. This removes the algebra, including the square root.
subtypes.trap: You may forget the ½ or ⅓ when you undo the formula, or stop before taking the square root. In a triangle, you may divide the area by the height without doubling it first.

subtypes.name: Scale factor: lengths vs. areas
subtypes.tell: The question has two figures, usually squares, rectangles or triangles, described as similar or with one side 'k times' the other. You are given a ratio of lengths or perimeters and asked for a ratio of areas, or the other way round. There may be a table comparing perimeters, or a question like 'the area is n times; what is n'.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the length scale factor k. A ratio of perimeters equals k. 2) Areas scale by k², and volumes by k³. 3) To find a matching side, set up a proportion using k. To find an area, multiply the known area by k².
subtypes.desmos: Mostly not needed. Try a side length of 1: the area of the scaled figure is k², so type k^2 for the given k. If k is large, Desmos squares it without error.
subtypes.trap: You may use k for the area instead of k². You may also treat a perimeter ratio as an area ratio, or square it when setting up a side proportion that needs k itself.

subtypes.name: Surface area, or surface area ↔ volume
subtypes.tell: The question says 'surface area'. Either you get a box's three dimensions and must find the total area of its faces, or you get a cube's surface area and must find its volume (or the reverse).
subtypes.method: 1) For a box, surface area = 2(lw + lh + wh). For a cube, surface area = 6s². 2) If you need to go from surface area to volume, divide by 6, take the square root to get s, then cube it.
subtypes.desmos: Type 2(lw+lh+wh) with the numbers substituted to check. For a cube chain, solving 6x² = SA and then cubing x is fast. It is only an arithmetic check.
subtypes.trap: You may count only three faces instead of six. For a cube, you may divide the surface area by 6 and give that as the volume, or skip the square root and cube the wrong number.

subtypes.name: Find the circle's radius from points, then circumference
subtypes.tell: The question shows points on a coordinate grid that 'define a circle' and asks for the circumference or area as kπ. No radius is given, so you have to find it from the positions of the points.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the centre. It is the point at the same distance from all the given points, often the midpoint of two points that sit opposite each other on the circle. 2) Count the distance from the centre to any one point to get r. 3) Circumference = 2πr, so k = 2r. For area, k = r².
subtypes.desmos: Plot the points. Then type (x−h)²+(y−k)²=r² with sliders for h, k and r, and adjust them until the circle passes through every point. Read r from the slider.
subtypes.trap: You may treat the distance between two opposite points (the diameter) as the radius, which doubles k. Or you may give the diameter or r² when the question asks for the circumference.

subtypes.name: Read center or radius from standard form (or write the equation)
subtypes.tell: You see an equation already in the form (x − h)² + (y − k)² = number, or you are given a center and radius and the choices are four such equations. The question asks for the center, the radius, the diameter, or which equation matches.
subtypes.method: 1) Flip the signs inside the brackets to get the center: (x − 3) means h = 3, and (x + 3) means h = −3. 2) Take the square root of the right-hand side to get r. If the question asks for the diameter, double r. 3) To write the equation, put h and k in with flipped signs and square the radius on the right.
subtypes.desmos: Type the equation exactly as given. The circle appears, and you can click its leftmost and rightmost points, or its top and bottom points, to read off the center and the diameter. For match-the-equation questions, graph each choice and see which one has the right center and size.
subtypes.trap: You report the right-hand side as the radius without taking its square root, or you keep the signs from inside the brackets so the center comes out with the wrong signs. On diameter questions, you give the radius and stop.

subtypes.name: Expanded circle equation: complete the square
subtypes.tell: The equation looks like x² + y² + ax + by + c = 0, with no brackets. Or the question says a circle has some center and radius and its equation is x² + y² + Dx + Ey + F = 0, and asks for one of the constants. Harder versions add a second circle with the same center and double the radius or diameter.
subtypes.method: 1) Group the x terms and the y terms. Add (half the x-coefficient)² and (half the y-coefficient)² to both sides. 2) Rewrite as (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² and read off the center and radius. 3) For a second circle, keep the center, scale r (doubling r multiplies r² by 4), then expand back out or substitute a given point if the question asks for a constant.
subtypes.desmos: Graph the expanded equation as given, because Desmos handles implicit equations, and read the center and radius from the picture. If there is an unknown constant, make it a slider and adjust it until the circle passes through the given point or has the required size. Do this as a check next to the algebra, because values that aren't whole numbers are hard to read off a graph.
subtypes.trap: You forget to add the completing-the-square constants to the right-hand side as well. Or, when the radius doubles, you double r² instead of multiplying it by 4. Or, when you expand back out, you drop the constant term that the new center creates.

subtypes.name: Arc length and central angle as a fraction of the circle
subtypes.tell: The question mentions an arc, a central angle, a circumference, or a radius or diameter. It asks for an arc length, an angle, the circumference, or what fraction of the circle an arc is. The angle may be in degrees or in radians.
subtypes.method: 1) Set up one proportion: arc length ÷ circumference = central angle ÷ 360° (or ÷ 2π in radians). 2) Fill in the two or three values you know and solve for the missing one. Remember that the degree measure of an arc equals its central angle. 3) Use d = 2r and C = 2πr = πd to move between radius, diameter and circumference.
subtypes.desmos: Not useful beyond working out the arithmetic. There is nothing to graph, so the whole task is spotting the proportion.
subtypes.trap: You mix up the arc's measure in degrees with its length. Or you divide by 180 instead of 360. Or you use the diameter where the formula needs the radius, which is off by a factor of 2.

subtypes.name: Tangent lines and radii (right angles, isosceles triangles)
subtypes.tell: You see the word 'tangent', or a triangle or quadrilateral with a vertex at the center and other vertices on the circle. In the xy-plane version, you are given a center and a point of tangency and asked for the tangent line's slope, or which point lies on the tangent line.
subtypes.method: 1) Any two segments from the center to the circle are radii, so they are equal. That makes triangles with a vertex at the center isosceles. 2) A tangent line meets the radius at a right angle. In coordinates, find the slope of the radius and take its negative reciprocal. 3) Two tangent segments drawn from the same outside point are equal. Use this to split the figure into two congruent right triangles and apply the Pythagorean theorem or area formulas.
subtypes.desmos: For coordinate versions, plot the center and the point of tangency. Then type y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) using the negative-reciprocal slope, and check which answer choice lies on that line. For geometric figures with no coordinates, Desmos only helps with the arithmetic.
subtypes.trap: You use the slope of the radius itself as the tangent's slope, or you take the reciprocal without changing the sign. In figures, you miss that the sides from the center are both radii, or that the angle between radius and tangent is 90°.

subtypes.name: Convert between radians and degrees
subtypes.tell: The question gives an angle in radians and asks for degrees, or the other way round. Harder versions hide the angle inside a difference or an expression.
subtypes.method: 1) Radians to degrees: multiply by 180/π. Degrees to radians: multiply by π/180. 2) Simplify the fraction. If the angle is a difference or an expression, convert the whole thing at once.
subtypes.desmos: Type the radian value times 180/π, or the degree value times π/180, and Desmos gives the decimal. To match a choice written in terms of π, divide your result by π to see the coefficient.
subtypes.trap: You multiply by the wrong factor (π/180 when you need 180/π). Or you leave π in a degree answer. Or you think of π as 3.14 degrees instead of 180°.

subtypes.name: Trig value of a radian angle using the unit circle
subtypes.tell: The question asks for sin, cos or tan of a radian angle. The angle is often larger than 2π, or built from another angle by multiplying it. The choices are special values like ±1/2, ±√2/2, ±√3/2, ±√3 or ±1.
subtypes.method: 1) Build the angle if it is defined through another one. Then subtract multiples of 2π (a full turn) until it is between 0 and 2π. 2) Find its reference angle and quadrant. 3) Use the unit-circle point (cos, sin) to get the value with the right sign. For tangent, divide y by x.
subtypes.desmos: Very effective. Desmos works in radians by default, so type the trig function of the angle exactly as written and compare the decimal with the choices worked out as decimals. Check that the degree setting is off.
subtypes.trap: You get the size right but the sign wrong because you misjudged the quadrant after reducing the angle. Or you use a sine value where the question asks for cosine.

subtypes.name: Expand, distribute, combine like terms
subtypes.tell: You're given a sum, difference or product of polynomials in parentheses, sometimes after being told what one or two letters or functions stand for, and asked which choice is equivalent. All four choices are simplified polynomials that differ only in a sign or one coefficient.
subtypes.method: 1) If you're given definitions (letters or f(x), g(x)), substitute them inside parentheses first. 2) Distribute every factor and every minus sign to every term inside its bracket. 3) Group terms by the same power of the variable (and the same variable) and add their coefficients.
subtypes.desmos: Type the original expression as y1 and each choice as y2. The right choice lies exactly on top of the original. You can also use a table and check that both give the same value at x = 2 and x = -1.
subtypes.trap: You apply a leading minus sign only to the first term inside the second bracket. Or you add unlike terms (x² with x, or xy with x²y) as if they were the same, or add exponents when you should only add coefficients.

subtypes.name: Pull out the greatest common factor
subtypes.tell: The given expression is a sum of two or three terms whose coefficients share a number, and often a power of x. Every choice is written as something times a bracket, so the question is really asking what the common factor is.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the GCF of the coefficients and the lowest power of each variable that every term shares. 2) Divide each term by that GCF to get what goes in the bracket. 3) Quick check: multiply the choice back out in your head.
subtypes.desmos: Graph the original and a choice. Matching curves confirm it, but it's faster to multiply the choice back out mentally, because these are easy questions.
subtypes.trap: You pull out a factor that isn't the greatest (the choice looks right but can still be factored). Or you forget to lower the exponent on the variable in each term, or drop a term whose quotient is 1.

subtypes.name: Special factoring patterns and vertex form
subtypes.tell: You see a trinomial whose first and last terms are perfect squares, a difference of two squares, a degree-4 expression with only even powers (a quadratic in x²), or choices written as (x ± h)² ± k. The question asks which is a factor or which is equivalent.
subtypes.method: 1) Check for a perfect square a² ± 2ab + b², a difference of squares a² − b², or substitute u = x² to turn a quartic into an ordinary quadratic. 2) For vertex-form choices, halve the x-coefficient to get h, square it, and adjust the constant so it still matches. 3) Expand the choice you pick to confirm the middle term.
subtypes.desmos: Graph the original. Its x-intercepts give the roots, and a root r means (x − r) is a factor. For vertex form, click the vertex and read (h, k) directly. This is often the fastest route.
subtypes.trap: You get the sign of h wrong in vertex form ((x − 3)² gives a vertex at x = +3). Or you pick factor pairs of the constant that multiply correctly but don't add to the middle coefficient, or forget to factor the coefficients themselves (the 9 in 9x²).

subtypes.name: Equivalent forms: solve for the unknown constant
subtypes.tell: The question says one expression 'is equivalent to' or 'can be rewritten as' another form containing constants a, b, c (or k), and asks for one constant or a combination of them. Often it's a grid-in, or the question asks which quantity 'must be an integer'.
subtypes.method: 1) Expand or simplify the side you're given until it's in the same form as the target. 2) Set the coefficients of each power of x (and the constant terms) equal to each other. 3) Solve the small system for the constant asked, then compute exactly what's requested, such as a sum or product, not just a single letter.
subtypes.desmos: Type the given expression and the target form with sliders for the unknown constants, and adjust until the graphs overlap. Or plug x = 0 into both sides (and x = 1 if you need more) to get equations for the constants quickly.
subtypes.trap: You find a but the question asks for a + b + c or a/b, so you stop one step early. Or a factor that multiplies the whole expression gets distributed to only one term before you compare coefficients.

subtypes.name: Add, simplify or divide rational expressions
subtypes.tell: The expression has a variable in the denominator, often with a note like 'where x > 0' or 'x ≠ some value'. You're asked to add two fractions, cancel a common factor, or rewrite a polynomial divided by a binomial as a quotient plus a remainder over the divisor.
subtypes.method: 1) To add or subtract, multiply each fraction to get the common denominator, then combine the numerators. 2) To simplify, factor the numerator and denominator and cancel the shared factor (the restriction tells you this is allowed). 3) To divide, rewrite the numerator as (divisor × something) + remainder and split it into two fractions, or use long or synthetic division.
subtypes.desmos: Graph the original and each choice for x in the allowed domain. The equivalent one overlaps everywhere except possibly at a hole. This is very reliable when the algebra is messy.
subtypes.trap: You add numerators and denominators straight across. Or you cancel a single term instead of a factor that multiplies the whole numerator and denominator, or you lose the remainder term in a division.

subtypes.name: Rewrite using exponent and radical rules
subtypes.tell: The expression mixes roots, fractional or negative exponents, or powers of powers. It's often multivariable with 'for positive values of' the variables, and the choices are the same thing written with radicals, fractional exponents or a different base. Sometimes you get a Roman-numeral format asking which forms are equivalent.
subtypes.method: 1) Convert every root to a fractional exponent (the nth root of x^m = x^(m/n)). 2) Apply the rules: multiply exponents when you raise a power to a power, add them when you multiply, subtract them when you divide, and apply the root to the coefficient too. 3) Convert back to the form the choices use and check each Roman-numeral statement separately.
subtypes.desmos: Assign a positive value to each variable (e.g. x = 2, y = 3) and evaluate the original and each choice as numbers. The equivalent ones give identical decimals. This works even when there are several variables.
subtypes.trap: You take the root of the variable but not the coefficient (or the reverse). Or you add exponents when you should multiply them, or apply the root twice. On Roman-numeral questions, you stop after confirming one statement.

subtypes.name: Largest population the results apply to
subtypes.tell: The stem ends by asking for the largest population or group the results can be generalized or applied to. The four choices are populations nested inside each other, from 'only the people in the sample' out to much broader groups. Sometimes a table is shown that includes only part of the sample, such as members who met some minimum threshold.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the exact group the sample was randomly drawn from, with every qualifier: the place, the age or level, the subgroup, and any minimum threshold stated for the data shown. 2) Pick the choice that matches that group exactly, keeping every qualifier. 3) If the subjects were randomly assigned to treatments but not randomly selected from a larger group, the results reach only as far as the group they were actually drawn from.
subtypes.trap: You pick a broader group, such as the whole region, all ages or everyone in the category, because it sounds more impressive. Or you pick the narrowest choice (only the sample) because you think a sample can never speak for anything larger. You also drop a qualifier, such as the threshold that defines which members appear in the table.

subtypes.name: Spot the biased sample
subtypes.tell: The sample was chosen by convenience (whoever was at one location), by self-selection (viewers or visitors who chose to respond), or from a subgroup that obviously has a stake in the answer. The choices argue about sample size, about whether the sample should be 'more' or 'less' of some group, or about whether the method is flawed or biased.
subtypes.method: 1) Compare the population the question wants to learn about with the group that was actually sampled. 2) If the sample was not randomly chosen from that whole population (it was self-selected, convenient or a special subgroup), choose the answer that calls it non-random or unrepresentative and possibly biased. 3) Rule out 'sample too small' unless the method was random and size really is the only issue.
subtypes.trap: You blame the sample size instead of how the sample was chosen. Or you accept a fix that swaps one unrepresentative subgroup for another, such as sampling only the opposite group. Or you treat a clear majority in a biased sample as proof about the whole population.

subtypes.name: What must be true from a random sample result
subtypes.tell: A random sample produces a percentage or a mean, and you are asked which statement(s) must be true, often in a Roman-numeral or numbered-list format. The statements claim the population has exactly that value, or that another sample would give exactly the same value, or that a different population would.
subtypes.method: 1) Remember that a sample statistic only estimates the population value; it is never guaranteed to be exact. 2) Reject any statement that says the population, a repeat sample or a different population has exactly the same number. 3) Usually the answer is 'none' or 'neither', unless a statement is hedged, for example 'approximately' or 'is an estimate of'.
subtypes.trap: You accept the claim that the exact sample value holds for the whole population because the sample was random. Or you accept that a new random sample would give the identical result. The key word is 'must', and a random sample only makes the estimate reasonable, not exact.

subtypes.name: Which conclusion the survey supports
subtypes.tell: A random sample was drawn from a specifically defined group, and a strong result is reported, such as a large majority. The four choices are full-sentence conclusions: some describe the sampled group, some describe a broader or different group, and some reverse the condition that defined the group.
subtypes.method: 1) Write down, in a few words, the defining condition of the group that was sampled. 2) Pick the conclusion about that same group, stated with a hedge such as 'most' rather than an exact figure. 3) Eliminate choices that widen the population or flip the defining condition.
subtypes.trap: You pick a choice that extends the result to everyone in a broader category. Or you pick one about the opposite group, reasoning that the opposite group would react the opposite way, which the data never tested.

subtypes.name: Cause and effect or just association
subtypes.tell: The stem describes either an experiment in which subjects were randomly assigned to treatment groups, or a study in which the researcher only recorded what people already did. The choices use words like 'causes', 'is associated with', 'improves' and 'is related to', often paired with different populations.
subtypes.method: 1) Ask whether the subjects were randomly assigned to conditions. If yes, a cause-and-effect conclusion is allowed. If no, only an association is allowed. 2) Ask whether they were randomly selected from a population. That decides how far the conclusion can be generalized. 3) Choose the answer that gets both parts right.
subtypes.trap: You accept a causal claim from observational data because the correlation looks strong. Or you mix up the two kinds of randomness: random selection lets you generalize, random assignment lets you claim a cause, and a correct answer can't claim one without having it.

subtypes.name: Scale a sample up to the population
subtypes.tell: You get a random sample with a count or percent that has some trait, plus a total population size, and the question asks for the 'best estimate' or 'expected' number in the whole group. The choices are whole numbers, sometimes written as sentences like 'exactly N' versus 'best estimate is N'. Some versions give a table, a per-unit mean (like items per plot), or ask for the complement or a winning margin.
subtypes.method: 1) Write the sample fraction as trait count over sample size. If the question asks about the complement, a difference between two groups, or totals across a two-way table, get that fraction first. 2) Multiply it by the population size. If you're given a per-unit mean, multiply the mean by the number of units instead. 3) Pick the choice that says 'best estimate', not 'exactly' or 'must'.
subtypes.desmos: Only as a calculator: type (count/sample)*population to check the arithmetic. It adds nothing beyond that.
subtypes.trap: You report the raw sample count as the population answer, or you multiply by the wrong group (for example, the sample size instead of the population). You pick 'exactly/must be' over 'best estimate'. Or you answer for the trait when the question asks for the people WITHOUT it, or for one candidate when it asks by how many that candidate wins.

subtypes.name: Interpret the margin-of-error interval
subtypes.tell: You're given an estimated mean or percent with an 'associated margin of error' and asked for the 'most appropriate/plausible conclusion' or the 'best interpretation'. The choices are sentences that mix 'between A and B', 'exactly X', 'greater/less than', or claims about ALL individual values or 'most' individuals.
subtypes.method: 1) Compute estimate − MOE and estimate + MOE. 2) Pick the choice that says the POPULATION mean or proportion (not individual values, and not the sample) is PLAUSIBLY between those two numbers. 3) Rule out any choice with 'exactly', 'not possible', 'every value' or 'all individuals', and any one-sided 'greater than' claim.
subtypes.desmos: Not needed. It's two mental additions plus reading the wording carefully, and a graph gives you nothing here.
subtypes.trap: You apply the interval to individual values ('all handbags weigh between…', 'every visitor hiked…') instead of the population MEAN. You pick a certainty word ('exactly', 'not possible'). You apply the interval to the sample instead of the population. Or you misread MOE as the percent of respondents who were misclassified.

subtypes.name: Turn a percent ± MOE into a range of counts
subtypes.tell: The estimate and margin of error are both given as percents, but the population is a stated total count. The question asks for a plausible NUMBER of items or people (often labeled with a variable), and the choices are numeric ranges or inequalities on that count.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the low and high percents: estimate − MOE and estimate + MOE. 2) Multiply each by the population total to get a count interval. 3) Choose the value or inequality that falls inside that count interval.
subtypes.desmos: Optional: type low%*N and high%*N to get both endpoints. You don't need anything more.
subtypes.trap: You add the MOE percent as a raw count (for example, ±2 items instead of ±2% of the total). You multiply by the sample size instead of the population. Or you use only the point estimate and pick a choice that lies just outside the true interval.

subtypes.name: Find the margin of error from a given interval
subtypes.tell: You're told the sample mean or percent AND the resulting 'between L and U' range, and the question asks what the margin of error is. The choices are single small numbers.
subtypes.method: 1) Subtract the sample value from the upper bound (or subtract the lower bound from the sample value). 2) Check that the other side gives the same distance. If the sample value isn't given, use (U − L)/2.
subtypes.desmos: Not useful: it's one subtraction.
subtypes.trap: You give the full width of the interval (U − L) instead of half of it. Or you give one of the endpoints themselves.

subtypes.name: How sample size changes the margin of error
subtypes.tell: You're comparing two samples from the same population with MOEs computed the same way, or a researcher is choosing between a smaller and a larger sample, or a sample size gets multiplied. The question asks why one MOE is bigger, what happens to the MOE, or what range the new MOE falls in.
subtypes.method: 1) Larger sample means smaller MOE, and smaller sample means larger MOE. The sample's percent or estimate is NOT the reason. 2) If the size is multiplied by k, the MOE is divided by √k. Doubling the size cuts the MOE to about 0.71 of its original, so it is smaller but NOT halved. Pick the range that fits.
subtypes.desmos: Type originalMOE/sqrt(2) (or /sqrt(k)) to place the new MOE in the correct range. Otherwise Desmos adds nothing.
subtypes.trap: You say the larger sample has the larger MOE. You credit the difference to the sample's higher percent in favor. Or, on the scaling version, you assume doubling the sample halves the MOE.

subtypes.name: Which population can the sample speak for
subtypes.tell: The sample was drawn from only one subgroup (one species, one class, one type), and the answer choices make claims about different scopes: the whole population, only that subgroup, the average, or a majority.
subtypes.method: 1) Identify exactly which group was randomly sampled. 2) Pick the choice that carries the sample statistic over to THAT group only, using the same statistic (a percent stays a percent) and hedged with 'approximately'.
subtypes.desmos: Not applicable: this is purely a reasoning question and involves no computation.
subtypes.trap: You extend the result to a broader population that wasn't sampled, such as all fish instead of the one species sampled. Or you turn a percent-above-a-threshold into a claim about the average or the majority.

subtypes.name: Solve a bare linear equation for x
subtypes.tell: You see one equation with only x in it (sometimes fractions, decimals, or a common factor like a group in parentheses on both terms). It asks for x itself, or asks which equation is equivalent to it. The answer choices are plain numbers, or it's a grid-in.
subtypes.method: 1) If the same grouped factor appears in every term, factor it out first; if there are fractions, multiply through by the common denominator. 2) Move the x-terms to one side and the constants to the other. 3) Divide by the coefficient. For 'which is equivalent', do the operation that turns the given equation into the form the choices are written in.
subtypes.desmos: Type the equation exactly as given. Desmos draws a vertical line at the solution, and you can tap it to read x. You can also graph y = left side and y = right side and read the x-coordinate of the intersection. This is fastest when the equation has fractions or decimals.
subtypes.trap: The wrong choices are what you get from a sign slip when you move a term across, from subtracting the coefficient when you should divide by it, or from the solution of a similar equation with one sign flipped. Plug your answer back in to check.

subtypes.name: Find the value of an expression, not x
subtypes.tell: It says 'If [equation], what is the value of' followed by something other than x: 3x, x − 4, 2x + 1, or a multiple of the whole left side. The trap choices include the value of x.
subtypes.method: 1) See whether the target expression is a multiple or shift of something already in the equation (for example, the target is half the left side, or equals the left side minus a constant). 2) If it is, get it in one move by dividing or subtracting on both sides. 3) If it isn't, solve for x and substitute.
subtypes.desmos: Solve for x as in a bare equation, then type the target expression with that x value (or define x = value on one line and type the expression on the next). It works, but it's slower than spotting the scaling.
subtypes.trap: You stop at x and choose it because it's listed. The other traps are the value of an intermediate expression, or the result of scaling only part of the equation.

subtypes.name: No solution / infinitely many solutions / find the constant
subtypes.tell: Look for the phrases 'has no solution', 'infinitely many solutions', or 'how many solutions', often with 'a and b are constants'. The equation has x on both sides, usually with parentheses. The choices are values of a constant, pairs of constants, Roman-numeral statements, or 'exactly one / none / infinitely many'.
subtypes.method: 1) Distribute and simplify both sides into the form (coefficient)x + (constant). 2) Infinitely many solutions: the x-coefficients are equal AND the constants are equal. No solution: the x-coefficients are equal and the constants are NOT equal. Exactly one: the x-coefficients differ. 3) Set up the matching conditions and solve for the constant(s). Anything the problem only rules out (≠) doesn't have to be true.
subtypes.desmos: Graph y = left side and y = right side, and put a slider on the unknown constant. Parallel lines mean no solution; lines that sit on top of each other mean infinitely many. For 'how many solutions' with no constants, graph both sides and see whether the lines coincide.
subtypes.trap: You make the constants match for a 'no solution' question, or you forget that 'no solution' also needs the constants to differ. You also drop a sign or forget to distribute the constant to every term. On must-be-true questions, you pick a statement that only could be true.

subtypes.name: Set up and solve a one-step context problem
subtypes.tell: The question is a short story with a starting amount and a constant rate: a fee plus a monthly charge, a quantity that drops by a fixed amount per time period, a perimeter with known sides, or a budget split between two purchases. It asks 'how many', 'after how many months/hours/days', or 'what is the length'. The answer is a single number.
subtypes.method: 1) Write starting amount + (rate)(unknown) = total. If the rate isn't given, find it first by dividing the change between two data points by the time between them. 2) Solve for the unknown. 3) Reread what's being asked: total time or additional time, the item count or the dollars.
subtypes.desmos: Graph y = start + rate·x and y = target, then click the intersection. This is useful when the numbers are messy decimals. For rate-from-two-points problems, you can enter the two points in a table and use a regression.
subtypes.trap: You answer a different quantity than the one asked: the extra hours instead of the total hours, the amount removed instead of the time, or the spending on one item instead of the count. You also forget to subtract the one-time fee or starting amount before dividing.

subtypes.name: Write the expression or equation for a situation
subtypes.tell: It asks 'Which of the following represents this situation' or 'in terms of n/w'. The answer choices are four algebraic expressions or equations built from the same numbers and variable in different arrangements.
subtypes.method: 1) Translate phrase by phrase: 'twice' means multiply by 2, 'more than' means add, 'longer than' means add to the other dimension, 'times the number of' means multiply that variable. 2) Build the total by adding the parts (for a perimeter, 2·length + 2·width). 3) Set it equal to the stated total if the question asks for an equation.
subtypes.desmos: It usually doesn't help, because there's nothing to solve. To check, pick a concrete value for the variable, work out the real answer by hand, and plug that value into each choice.
subtypes.trap: You mix up 'more than' with 'times' (writing 3n instead of 2n + 3), or you reverse subtraction order. You also use a partial sum (one length plus one width), the area formula when perimeter is asked, or attach the multiplier to the wrong variable.

subtypes.name: Plug in the known quantity
subtypes.tell: You get a finished equation in two variables tied to a real-world context, you're told the value of one quantity, and you're asked how many of the other. Sometimes the equation isn't printed and you have to write it first from two per-unit rates and a total, with one amount already fixed.
subtypes.method: 1) If there's no equation, write rate1·a + rate2·b = total. 2) Put the given number in for its variable. 3) Solve the resulting one-variable equation for the other.
subtypes.desmos: Type the equation, then type a vertical line x = given value (or a horizontal line y = value if the given quantity is on the y-axis) and click the intersection to read the other coordinate. It is quicker to do by hand if the arithmetic is clean.
subtypes.trap: You substitute the given number for the wrong variable because you matched it to the first letter in the equation instead of reading which letter stands for which quantity. Or you forget a unit conversion, such as rates given per 30 minutes when the question asks about hours.

subtypes.name: Translate the story into an equation
subtypes.tell: The question ends with 'which equation represents this situation'. All four choices are ax + by = c forms using the same numbers in different places. The stem gives two per-item values (price, points, speed, rate) and a total.
subtypes.method: 1) Pair each per-item value with the variable that counts that item. 2) Add the two products and set the sum equal to the total. 3) Pick the choice that matches, checking which coefficient sits on which variable. For a 'total = part + other part' story, the whole goes alone on one side.
subtypes.trap: The wrong choices swap the coefficients between the variables, multiply the total by a rate, or put the rates on the wrong side of the equation. If you skim for 'the right numbers' you'll pick the swapped version. For percent-increase stories, you might use the percentages themselves instead of the growth factors (1 + r).

subtypes.name: What does the coefficient mean
subtypes.tell: You're given a context equation ax + by = c and asked how much more (or what) one unit of one item is worth than another, or what a number in the equation represents. The answer is a small number built from the coefficients, not a solution for x or y.
subtypes.method: 1) Each coefficient is the value of one unit of the item its variable counts. 2) For a 'how many more' question, subtract the two coefficients in the order asked. 3) The constant on the other side is the total, not a per-item amount.
subtypes.desmos: Desmos doesn't help here. Nothing needs solving; you only have to read what each coefficient means.
subtypes.trap: You try to solve for x or y, or you answer with a single coefficient, the sum of the coefficients, or the total. Watch the direction of the subtraction when the question says one item is worth more than the other.

subtypes.name: Parallel / perpendicular slope
subtypes.tell: The words 'perpendicular to' or 'parallel to' appear. Line one is given as an equation in standard form, as two points, or as a graph, and you're asked for the slope of line two, or for a point on line two.
subtypes.method: 1) Get the slope of the given line: rearrange to y = mx + b (for Ax + By = C, the slope is -A/B), or use rise over run between two points. 2) Parallel keeps the same slope; perpendicular flips the fraction and changes the sign. 3) If you need a point, build y = mx + b using the given intercept or point and substitute.
subtypes.desmos: Graph the given equation and click two lattice points to read the slope. You can check a perpendicular answer by graphing it and seeing a right angle, but the negative reciprocal is faster by hand.
subtypes.trap: The wrong choices include the original slope, its reciprocal without the sign change, and the negative without the reciprocal. In standard form, you might also read A (or -A) as the slope instead of -A/B.

subtypes.name: Match the equation to a table or graph
subtypes.tell: You're given a table of x and y values or a graphed line and asked which equation represents the relationship, or you're given an equation and asked which table fits it. All four choices are equations (or tables), sometimes with an unknown positive constant.
subtypes.method: 1) Take two clear points and find the slope, then the y-intercept (the y-value where x = 0 if the table has it). 2) Write y = mx + b, or rearrange to match the choices. 3) Faster option: substitute two points into each choice and keep the one that works for both.
subtypes.desmos: Type the table into a Desmos table, type each choice as an equation, and see which line passes through every point. For a graph with labelled points, plot those points the same way.
subtypes.trap: A choice that passes through one point but not the other, a slope computed as run over rise, or an intercept with the wrong sign. When a constant k appears, you might treat it as a number instead of reading it from the graph's labelled intercept.

subtypes.name: Read the slope or intercept
subtypes.tell: It's a short stem: 'what is the slope of the graph of…', 'what is the y-intercept of the line shown', or 'the y-intercept is (0, k), find k'. You're given a single equation, often in standard form, or a single graph.
subtypes.method: 1) For the y-intercept, set x = 0 and solve for y (or read where the line crosses the y-axis). 2) For the slope, solve for y and take the coefficient of x (for Ax + By = C, it's -A/B).
subtypes.desmos: Type the equation and click where the line crosses the y-axis; Desmos labels the point. For the slope, click two grid points on the line and compute rise over run.
subtypes.trap: You give the x-intercept instead of the y-intercept, give the whole ordered pair when a single coordinate is asked, or read the slope straight off standard form as A or B without dividing and changing the sign.

subtypes.name: Build the line, then use it
subtypes.tell: You're given a y-intercept plus another point (or a table), sometimes with a shift up or down, and asked for a missing coordinate of a third point, or the x-intercept of the new line. The question has more than one step and is usually hard.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the slope from the two known points and write y = mx + b. 2) Apply any shift to b (shifting down by k units changes b to b - k). 3) Substitute the known coordinate of the target point, or set y = 0 for the x-intercept, and solve.
subtypes.desmos: Enter y = mx + b with m and b as sliders, adjust until the line passes through the given points, then trace to the target x-value or to the x-intercept. For a shift, type the second line as y = (first line) - k.
subtypes.trap: You shift the x-intercept by the translation amount instead of shifting b, you solve for the original line's intercept and forget the shift, or you mix up which coordinate of the target point is unknown.

subtypes.name: Plug in and evaluate
subtypes.tell: You get a fully defined function with no unknown constants and a single input value, and you're asked for the output. The wrong choices are often the outputs for nearby or related inputs.
subtypes.method: 1) Put the given input in for x, keeping parentheses around negatives and fractions. 2) Simplify in order of operations. 3) Check that your number is the output, not the input or some other value from the problem.
subtypes.desmos: Type the function exactly as given, then type f(value) on a new line to get the result instantly. This is useful for fractions and negatives.
subtypes.trap: You substitute into the wrong place or drop a negative sign. The trap is also that you solve f(x) = value when the question asks for f(value), or the reverse.

subtypes.name: Find the hidden constant from one known output
subtypes.tell: The function has a letter constant (a slope or intercept named with a letter) and you're given one input-output pair in f(number) = number form. You're asked for the constant, or for a different output once the constant is known.
subtypes.method: 1) Substitute the known input and output into the rule. 2) Solve the resulting one-variable equation for the constant. 3) If the question asks for a new output, rewrite the function with the constant filled in and evaluate at the new input.
subtypes.desmos: Enter the rule with the constant as a slider, or enter the equation you get after substituting and let Desmos solve for the constant. Then type f(new input). This helps when the numbers are messy.
subtypes.trap: You stop after finding the constant when the question asked for a second output. Or you mix up the input and output when substituting.

subtypes.name: Build the line from two points, a table, or slope plus a point
subtypes.tell: You're given two coordinate points, a table of x and f(x) values, or a slope and one point. The answer choices are equations in slope-intercept form, or you're asked for one coefficient, the intercept, a missing table entry, or a combination such as a sum or product of the constants.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the slope from any two rows or points: change in output over change in input. 2) Get the intercept from the row where x is 0, or by substituting one point into y = mx + b. 3) Answer exactly what's asked: the whole equation, one constant, a combination, or a new output.
subtypes.desmos: Enter the points or table as a table, then fit a regression y1 ~ m x1 + b to read off m and b exactly. You can also graph each answer choice and see which one passes through every point.
subtypes.trap: You compute the slope as change in x over change in y, or with the subtraction order mismatched. The trap is also that you give m or b when the question asked for a combination of them, or you pick a choice that only fits one row of the table.

subtypes.name: Write the linear model from a word description
subtypes.tell: A real-world scenario describes a starting amount plus or minus a fixed amount per unit (per second, per year, per foot, per gallon). There is no table or graph, and all four answer choices are equations or functions built from the same numbers in different arrangements.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the starting value: the amount when the input is 0, which becomes the constant term. 2) Find the rate per single unit, dividing if the rate is given per several units, and give it the right sign. 3) Write output = start ± rate × input. Adjust the input if the rate only starts after a threshold, such as (x − n).
subtypes.desmos: Mostly unhelpful for building the model itself. You can check a choice by graphing it and testing one concrete case you can work out by hand, such as the value at input 0 or at input 1.
subtypes.trap: You swap the starting value and the rate, or use + when the quantity is decreasing. The trap is also that you multiply by the 'per n units' figure instead of dividing, ignore a doubling or repetition, or forget that the per-unit charge only applies beyond an initial block.

subtypes.name: Say what the slope or intercept means
subtypes.tell: You're given a context model, as an equation or a graph with labeled axes, and asked what a coefficient or constant represents. The wording is 'each additional', 'per', 'initial', 'at the start', or 'when none'.
subtypes.method: 1) For 'each' or 'per' questions, the answer is the slope: read the coefficient, or compute rise over run between two clear grid points on the graph. 2) For 'initial' or 'starting' questions, the answer is the output when the input is 0, which is the y-intercept. 3) Attach the sign and units the question asks for.
subtypes.desmos: For a given equation, graph it and click the y-intercept, or read the coefficient directly. For a pictured graph Desmos adds little. Just pick two lattice points.
subtypes.trap: You report the intercept when the slope was asked, or the reverse. The trap is also that you give a negative rate when the question asks how much is 'used' or 'lost' per unit, which is the magnitude.

subtypes.name: How much does the output change?
subtypes.tell: The question asks 'by how much' the output increases or decreases when the input increases by some amount, or asks for the change over an interval on a graph. It doesn't ask for the output at a single point.
subtypes.method: 1) Change in output = slope × change in input. The constant term cancels, so ignore it. 2) On a graph, read the y-values at the two ends of the interval and subtract.
subtypes.desmos: Evaluate f(a + h) − f(a) for any convenient a to confirm. For a pictured graph, reading two points by hand is faster.
subtypes.trap: You plug the change amount straight into the function and include the intercept. Or on a graph you report the output at the end of the interval instead of the difference between the two ends.

subtypes.name: Read a feature off the graph, or match an equation to its graph
subtypes.tell: There is a graph with no real-world story and you're asked for an intercept. Or you're given an equation and all four answer choices are graphs.
subtypes.method: 1) For an intercept, find where the line crosses the named axis: the y-intercept is where x = 0. 2) To match a graph, use the y-intercept to rule out choices, then check the sign and steepness of the slope, stepping 1 right and m up.
subtypes.desmos: Graph the given equation and compare it with the pictured choices, or click the axis crossings to read the intercepts exactly.
subtypes.trap: You give the x-intercept when the question asked for the y-intercept, or write the point with its coordinates reversed. When matching, you pick a graph with the right intercept but the wrong slope sign.

subtypes.name: Parallel lines / intersecting lines: one angle relationship
subtypes.tell: You see a figure with two parallel lines cut by a transversal, or just two crossing lines. Two angles are marked, one numeric or both as expressions, and you're asked for a variable. The two marked angles are either in matching positions or next to each other on a straight line. A harder version has no figure: it describes the eight angles a transversal makes and asks which expression can or cannot equal a sum of four of them.
subtypes.method: 1) Name the relationship between the two marked angles: vertical, corresponding, or alternate interior means equal; a linear pair or same-side interior/exterior means they add to 180. 2) Write that single equation and solve it. 3) For the no-figure version, remember a transversal across parallel lines makes only two distinct angle measures, x and 180 - x. Any four of the eight angles sum to a·x + b(180 - x) with a + b = 4. Test each choice against that form.
subtypes.desmos: Mostly unnecessary, because the equation is one linear step. If the angles are expressions like 3x + 10 and 5x - 30, you can type each side as y = ... and read the x-value where the lines cross. For the four-angle-sum version, Desmos doesn't help; you need the structural argument.
subtypes.trap: You set angles equal when they are actually supplementary, or the reverse. The wrong choices usually include the other angle's measure, 180 minus the correct answer, or the complement (90 minus the answer).

subtypes.name: Triangle angle sum: find the missing angle
subtypes.tell: The question involves a single triangle, drawn or described in words. Two angles are given (or their sum), or all three are given as expressions in one variable, and you're asked for the third angle or the variable. An isosceles condition such as two equal sides may be the hidden extra fact.
subtypes.method: 1) Write angle1 + angle2 + angle3 = 180. If two sides are equal, set the two base angles opposite those sides equal first. 2) Solve for the variable. 3) Check whether the question asks for the variable or for an angle built from it, and substitute if it asks for the angle.
subtypes.desmos: Type the sum of the angle expressions = 180 and Desmos returns x directly. That saves little time over doing it by hand, but it avoids arithmetic slips when the coefficients are fractions.
subtypes.trap: You find x and stop when the question asked for an angle expression like 2x + 5, or the reverse. You subtract only one given angle from 180. Or you miss that equal sides force equal opposite angles and treat the triangle as unsolvable.

subtypes.name: Multi-step angle chase through a composite figure
subtypes.tell: The figure has several lines, often parallel lines plus a pair of crossing lines, two triangles sharing a vertex, or a polygon with one pair of parallel sides. The angle you want is not next to any given angle, so at least two facts have to be linked. These are often free-response questions at hard difficulty, sometimes with fractional answers.
subtypes.method: 1) Mark every given value on the figure and look for a triangle that contains the target angle or a vertical or supplementary partner of it. 2) Move known values into that triangle using vertical, linear-pair, or parallel-line relationships, one link at a time. For a polygon, extend a side to make a transversal. 3) Close with the 180 triangle sum or a straight-line sum, then convert back to the target angle if the target sits outside the triangle.
subtypes.desmos: Not useful for the reasoning, which is spatial. At most, use it to solve the final linear equation if the given values are expressions.
subtypes.trap: You stop at an intermediate angle, such as the triangle's interior angle, when the question asks for the exterior or supplementary angle next to it. The wrong choices often include that intermediate value. The other common error is assuming a right angle or a parallel pair that the question never states.

subtypes.name: Similar / congruent figures: read off corresponding parts
subtypes.tell: The question says two triangles or polygons are similar, congruent, or related by a dilation, and gives the vertex correspondence, either by listing it or by letter order. It asks for an angle in one figure using information about the other figure. A scale factor or side lengths are often included as a distraction when the question asks for an angle. A variant has a segment drawn parallel to one side inside a triangle and asks for a side length.
subtypes.method: 1) Match vertices using the letter order or the stated correspondence, not the picture. 2) Corresponding angles are equal, and the scale factor never changes angles. If the matched angle isn't given directly, find it with the 180 triangle sum, using any right angle. 3) For side lengths when there's a parallel segment: the small and large triangles are similar (AA), so set up small/large = small/large using matching sides and solve.
subtypes.desmos: It doesn't help with angle questions; the answer comes from matching vertices. For the side-length variant, you can type the proportion as an equation to solve it, but cross-multiplying by hand is just as fast.
subtypes.trap: You apply the scale factor to an angle measure, or match vertices by where they sit in the drawing instead of by the stated order. Wrong choices include the given angle's complement or supplement and the given angle multiplied by the scale factor.

subtypes.name: Which extra fact is sufficient to prove it?
subtypes.tell: The question stem asks which additional information is sufficient to prove something: two lines are parallel, two triangles are similar, or two triangles are congruent. Some facts are already given, and each choice (or each of the Roman-numeral statements I/II/III) adds a condition. The answer is a condition, not a number.
subtypes.method: 1) List what you already have, such as one pair of equal angles or two side lengths. 2) Name the criterion you need to finish. Parallel lines need corresponding or alternate interior angles equal, or same-side interior angles supplementary. Similarity needs AA, SAS~ (equal included angle and proportional sides), or SSS~. Congruence needs SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, or HL. 3) Test each option: does adding it complete the criterion? Remember that a pair of vertical angles or a linear pair is always true, so it proves nothing about parallel lines. Knowing a triangle's other angles lets you get the third from the 180 sum.
subtypes.desmos: Null. This is a logic question about criteria, with nothing to graph or compute.
subtypes.trap: You pick a condition that is true whenever the lines cross (vertical angles, a linear pair), so it can't prove parallelism. For similarity you accept proportional sides when the equal angle isn't the one between them (SSA). For congruence you accept angles alone (AAA), or a right angle without the hypotenuse-leg or side matching it needs.

subtypes.name: Find the constant from the number of solutions
subtypes.tell: You're told a quadratic contains an unknown constant and has exactly one solution, no real solutions, or more than one real solution, and you're asked for the constant, or the largest or smallest value it can take. Sometimes it's framed as a parabola meeting a horizontal line or another line exactly once.
subtypes.method: 1) Move everything to one side so it reads ax^2 + bx + c = 0, and read off a, b and c, which may still contain the constant. 2) Set b^2 - 4ac = 0 for exactly one solution, < 0 for none, or > 0 for two. 3) Solve for the constant. If it has to be an integer, take the boundary integer on the correct side of the inequality.
subtypes.desmos: Type the equation with the constant as a slider, for example y = (left side) - (right side), and slide until the parabola just touches the x-axis (one solution) or clears it (none). If it's a line meeting a parabola, graph both and slide until they're tangent. You can also type b^2-4ac with the slider and read its sign.
subtypes.trap: The equation isn't in standard form yet, so you read a, b or c off the wrong side, or you forget the minus sign when moving a term. On inequality versions you also get the direction wrong (< 0 means none, > 0 means two) or pick the integer just outside the allowed range.

subtypes.name: Solve a bare quadratic
subtypes.tell: It's a single equation with an x^2 term and no unknown constants. The question asks for 'a solution', 'the positive solution' or 'what values satisfy', and the choices are specific numbers, sometimes pairs with radicals.
subtypes.method: 1) If there's no x term, isolate x^2 and take ± the square root. 2) Otherwise, get it into standard form and factor. If it doesn't factor cleanly, or the choices contain radicals, use the quadratic formula. 3) Pick the root the question asks for, such as the positive one.
subtypes.desmos: Graph y = left side - right side, or type both sides as separate curves, and click the x-intercepts or intersection points. This is fastest when the roots are ugly radicals: match the decimals to the choices.
subtypes.trap: You forget the negative root, or you take the square root before isolating x^2. The wrong choices are usually the positive root of a nearby equation with a sign flipped or a coefficient left undivided.

subtypes.name: Sum of the solutions and unknown-coefficient roots
subtypes.tell: You're asked for the sum of the solutions, a combination of roots from several equations, or a constant that makes the solutions add to a given value. Alternatively, the equation carries letters as coefficients and the choices are expressions, or you pick which of several expressions are solutions (I/II/III).
subtypes.method: 1) Rewrite in standard form ax^2 + bx + c = 0. For a quadratic, the sum of the roots is -b/a, so you often don't need the roots themselves. 2) If a common factor appears on both sides, don't divide it away: move everything to one side and factor it out so that root isn't lost. 3) For higher degree, factor completely with the zero product property, list every root including ±√ roots, then add them or set the sum equal to the target.
subtypes.desmos: Partly helpful. With numeric coefficients, graph it and add the x-intercepts. With letter coefficients, turn them into sliders, check the choices against a trial value, and confirm the relationship holds as you move the sliders.
subtypes.trap: You divide both sides by a factor that contains x and lose a solution. Or you use +b/a instead of -b/a, or forget to expand and combine terms before reading b and a. On sums, you might also drop a root, since ±√k roots cancel in the sum but still count.

subtypes.name: Rearrange a formula for one variable
subtypes.tell: The equation relates several letters, often a named real-world formula with fractions, reciprocals or a squared variable. The question asks 'which equation expresses X in terms of...' or 'which is equivalent to X', and every choice is an expression in the other letters.
subtypes.method: 1) Clear the fractions by multiplying through by the common denominator. 2) Collect every term containing the target variable on one side, factor that variable out if it appears more than once, then divide. 3) If the target is squared, take the square root and use the stated positivity to keep only the positive root. If you solved for 1/X, take reciprocals at the end.
subtypes.desmos: Usually slow, but it works as a check: pick numbers for all the other variables, compute the target from the original equation, and see which choice gives the same value.
subtypes.trap: You 'undo' a sum of fractions term by term, for example flipping 1/a + 1/b into a + b, or you divide before collecting the target variable's terms. You might also forget the reciprocal step or drop a subtraction's sign while isolating.

subtypes.name: Rational or radical equations and extraneous roots
subtypes.tell: The variable sits under a square root or in a denominator, and the equation may include a constant with a stated sign. The question asks for 'the solution', 'one of the solutions', or a constant that leaves exactly one real solution.
subtypes.method: 1) For fractions, multiply by the denominator, or cancel a common factor while noting the value x can't take. For radicals, isolate the root and square both sides. 2) Solve the resulting polynomial. 3) Substitute each candidate into the original equation and throw out any that make a denominator zero or make the radical side negative.
subtypes.desmos: Graph each side as its own curve and read off the intersections. Extraneous roots simply won't show up, which makes this a reliable check against the squaring trap.
subtypes.trap: You keep an extraneous root. That means a value that zeroes a denominator, or a squared-in solution where the square root would have to equal a negative number. The wrong choices usually include exactly that value.

subtypes.name: Linear–quadratic system on a graph
subtypes.tell: You get a graph of a parabola and a line and must find the solution (the intersection), or you get equations and must pick the matching graph, or you get a graph and must pick the matching system. The choices are either four graphs or four systems of equations.
subtypes.method: 1) The solution is the intersection point, so read its coordinates. 2) To match equations to a graph, compare features one at a time: the parabola's vertex from vertex form (or its intercepts and direction of opening), and the line's slope and y-intercept. 3) Eliminate choices that fail any one feature.
subtypes.desmos: Very effective. Type each choice's system and see which one reproduces the picture, or type the given system and compare it with the choice graphs. Click the intersection to get the exact point.
subtypes.trap: You flip the vertex's horizontal sign: in (x - h)^2 the vertex is at +h. Or you mix up slope and y-intercept, or report an axis intercept of one curve instead of the point where the two curves cross.

subtypes.name: Solve a line–quadratic system algebraically
subtypes.tell: Two equations are given with no graph, one linear and one quadratic, or one that gives y directly. The question asks which ordered pair is a solution, or for a value of x, y or a combination of them at the intersection.
subtypes.method: 1) Substitute the expression for y, or for the simpler variable, into the other equation. 2) Solve the resulting quadratic in one variable by factoring out a common factor or using the formula. 3) Put each x back into the simpler equation to get y. With choices, testing each ordered pair in both equations can be faster.
subtypes.desmos: Type both equations and click the intersection points to read the ordered pairs directly. This is usually the fastest route on multiple choice.
subtypes.trap: You find x but then report a pair whose y came from the wrong equation, or you pick a pair that satisfies only one equation. Dividing by x instead of factoring it out also loses the x = 0 solution.

subtypes.name: Plug in or solve for the input
subtypes.tell: You're given a function rule, often with a power, root or fraction, and asked either for its value at a specific input or for the input that gives a stated output. The answer choices are plain numbers, and the wrong ones are usually the result at a nearby input or its reciprocal.
subtypes.method: 1) Check which is given: if the input is given, substitute it into every x. If the output is given, set the expression equal to it. 2) To solve backwards, undo operations in reverse: subtract constants, divide by the coefficient, then take the root. 3) Check your answer by substituting it back.
subtypes.desmos: Type the function as f(x)=..., then type f(value) to get the output. To go backwards, graph y=target alongside f(x) and click the intersection to read x.
subtypes.trap: It tests whether you mix up 'the value of f when x is k' with 'the value of x when f is k'. It also catches order-of-operations slips, like squaring before multiplying by a negative, or forgetting the negative root.

subtypes.name: Read a feature straight off the graph
subtypes.tell: There is a graph and no equation. You're asked for its y-intercept, vertex, maximum or minimum, and the answer is a coordinate pair or a single number.
subtypes.method: 1) Name the feature: the y-intercept is where x = 0, and the vertex is the highest or lowest turning point. 2) Follow the gridlines to that point and read both coordinates, counting the scale on each axis.
subtypes.desmos: Not needed. There is no equation to enter, and reading the grid is faster.
subtypes.trap: You swap the coordinates, read the x-intercept when asked for the y-intercept, or misread an axis scale that goes up in 2s, 5s or 10s.

subtypes.name: What does this number or point mean in the story?
subtypes.tell: The function models something real, such as height over time, a population or revenue. You're asked for the 'best interpretation' of an intercept, a marked point, a constant in the equation, or f(0). Every answer choice is a sentence about the context.
subtypes.method: 1) Turn the feature into math: the y-intercept means input = 0, an x-intercept means output = 0, a vertex is a maximum or minimum, and a marked point means output = y when input = x. 2) Replace each variable with its units and meaning from the problem ('when 0 years have passed', 'when the height is 0 feet'). 3) Choose the sentence that says exactly that, with the numbers in the right roles.
subtypes.desmos: This is rarely useful. The question tests meaning, not calculation. At most, you can graph the model to see which intercept is positive.
subtypes.trap: The wrong choices reverse the input and output (the time is x, the height is y), call the starting value a minimum or maximum, describe the base of an exponential as an amount added each year, or give the vertex meaning when the question asks about the intercept.

subtypes.name: Write or use an exponential growth or decay model
subtypes.tell: The problem uses words like 'doubles every __ minutes', 'decreases by __% each year', or 'increases by a factor of', or it shows a table where each output is multiplied by the same number. You're asked for the function, a constant in it, a later value, or when a threshold is reached.
subtypes.method: 1) Write the model as y = (starting amount)·(growth factor)^(t / time per step). The growth factor is 1 + r for growth and 1 − r for decay, with r as a decimal. 2) Get the starting amount from the value at t = 0, or from a table row. If the table has no row for t = 0, work backwards to it. 3) Substitute the input you need, or set the model equal to the target and solve, testing the answer choices if that's quicker.
subtypes.desmos: Enter the candidate models from the answer choices and check them against two known points. Or graph the model with a horizontal line at the target value and read where they cross. To fit a table, enter it and use y1 ~ a·b^x1.
subtypes.trap: It catches using 0.02 as the factor instead of 0.98, forgetting to divide the exponent by the doubling or step interval, choosing a linear model for a percent change, and taking the first table row as the starting amount when it isn't the value at t = 0.

subtypes.name: Use the vertex and symmetry of a parabola
subtypes.tell: You're asked when a quadratic reaches its maximum or minimum, which value a coefficient could take given the vertex and the number of x-intercepts, or when a projectile comes back to a height it had earlier.
subtypes.method: 1) Get the vertex x-coordinate from x = −b/(2a), from vertex form, or as the midpoint of the two roots. 2) Use symmetry: a height reached at t₁ is reached again at 2·(vertex t) − t₁. 3) For 'could be the value' questions, write vertex form, check the direction of opening needed for the stated number of x-intercepts, then expand to test the coefficient.
subtypes.desmos: This is very useful. Graph the quadratic and click the turning point to read the vertex. Add a slider for any unknown constant and watch how the vertex and intercepts change.
subtypes.trap: You choose an x-intercept or the y-value of the vertex when the question asks for the x at the minimum. You also get the sign in −b/(2a) or in vertex form (x − h) wrong, or you ignore that the parabola must open away from the axis to cross it twice.

subtypes.name: Zeros ↔ factors
subtypes.tell: The question mentions zeros, roots or x-intercepts of a polynomial. You're given them and asked for a coefficient or constant term, given the factored form and asked which value is NOT an intercept, or given intercepts containing an unknown constant.
subtypes.method: 1) Each zero r gives a factor (x − r). Write the function as a product of those factors. 2) Expand only as much as you need: the constant term is the product of the −r values times the leading coefficient. 3) To find an unknown intercept, substitute that point and solve with the output set to 0.
subtypes.desmos: Graph the factored form and click the x-intercepts. For a missing constant, use a slider and match the intercepts. Checking an answer choice this way takes seconds.
subtypes.trap: You write the factor as (x + r) instead of (x − r), which flips signs. You also forget to solve inside a factor with a coefficient, like (3x − 2), where the zero is 2/3, not 2. Or you miss the sign of the product when there is an odd number of negative zeros.

subtypes.name: Find the unknown constants from given points
subtypes.tell: The function has letters for its constants. You're told it passes through certain points, has a certain y-intercept, or matches a table of values. You're asked for one constant, a combination of constants, or which equation defines it.
subtypes.method: 1) Use the y-intercept first. Setting x = 0 usually gives one constant right away. 2) Substitute each remaining point to get an equation in the constants, then solve the resulting small system. 3) For 'which equation' questions, test the table points in each answer choice. Usually one or two points rule out everything but the answer.
subtypes.desmos: Enter the table and fit it with a regression such as y1 ~ ax1^2 + bx1 + c. This returns the constants directly. Or graph each answer choice and see which one goes through all the points.
subtypes.trap: The question asks for a combination such as a + b, or for one constant, and the wrong choices are the other constant or a partial sum. You also slip on signs when you substitute a negative x into a squared term.

subtypes.name: Write a function for a geometric quantity
subtypes.tell: The problem describes a shape whose dimensions depend on each other ('the length is 3 more than the width') and asks for a function giving the area or volume in terms of one named variable. The answer choices are expanded or factored polynomials.
subtypes.method: 1) Write every dimension in terms of the variable the question names. If the length is the input, the width is length − 3, not width + 3. 2) Multiply the dimensions using the formula for the shape. 3) Compare with the answer choices, expanding only if they are expanded.
subtypes.desmos: This helps a little. Pick a test value for the variable, work out the true volume by hand, and evaluate each answer choice at that value to see which one matches.
subtypes.trap: You write the function in terms of the wrong dimension (width instead of length), so the offset has the wrong sign. You also forget to multiply by the fixed height, or add the dimensions when you should multiply them.

subtypes.name: Read a value off a graph or table
subtypes.tell: You get a bar graph, frequency table, category table or box plot, and the question asks for one count, a difference or sum of two counts, the category with a given frequency, the max or min value, or the median line of a box plot. No calculation beyond one addition or subtraction.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the exact row, bar or line the question names. 2) Read its height, frequency or position off the scale. 3) If asked, add or subtract the two readings.
subtypes.desmos: null: nothing to graph. You only read a value off the display and maybe do one subtraction.
subtypes.trap: You read the wrong column of a frequency table, for example giving the largest frequency when the question wants the largest data value. Or you take a box edge (Q1/Q3) instead of the middle line as the median. Or you misread the gridline scale on a bar.

subtypes.name: Compute the mean or median of a given set
subtypes.tell: A short list, a row of table values, or a frequency table is given, and the question asks directly for 'the mean' or 'the median'. The wrong answer choices include the median, range, minimum or maximum of the same data.
subtypes.method: Mean: add the values (weighted by frequency if it is a table) and divide by the count. Median: sort the values first, then take the middle one, or average the two middle ones if the count is even. From a frequency table, count cumulative frequencies to find the middle position.
subtypes.desmos: Type mean([...]) or median([...]) with the values. For a frequency table, enter the values in one column and the frequencies in another, then use mean(L1,L2) or the table's stats. This makes long or decimal-heavy lists instant.
subtypes.trap: You take the middle of an unsorted list as the median. Or you average the distinct values in a frequency table without weighting by frequency. Or you pick the choice that is actually the median, range or max.

subtypes.name: Work backward from a mean to a missing value
subtypes.tell: One data value is an unknown (x, or 'the value not shown'), and you are told the mean, or that two sets' means are equal or differ by a set amount. Or two groups' means and sizes are given and you need the combined mean. Hard versions add median and range conditions on an ordered list with several constants.
subtypes.method: 1) Convert each mean to a total: sum = mean × count. 2) Set up the equation (known sum + x = required total) and solve. For combined groups, add the two totals and divide by the combined count; do not average the two means. 3) With median or range conditions, use position (middle term) and max − min to pin down constants first.
subtypes.desmos: Type the equation, e.g. (a+b+c+d+x)/5 = 74, and read the x-intercept or the solved value. Helpful for messy decimals, less so for multi-condition ordered-list questions.
subtypes.trap: You average the two group means as if the groups were the same size. Or you forget to include the unknown in the count. Or, when the mean must be an integer in a range, you stop before checking which candidate satisfies every constraint.

subtypes.name: Compare standard deviation or spread without calculating
subtypes.tell: The words 'standard deviation' or 'spread' appear. You get two histograms or dot plots, or answer choices that are lists (often all symmetric about the same center), and must say which is smaller or larger or whether they are equal.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the center of each set. It is often identical by symmetry. 2) Ask which set has more of its values bunched near the center and fewer out at the extremes; that one has the smaller SD. 3) A shifted but identical shape means equal SD.
subtypes.desmos: Enter each list and use stdev() to confirm if you are unsure, but the visual 'distance from center' judgment is faster and is what the question tests.
subtypes.trap: You judge spread by range alone or by the number of distinct values instead of how much data sits far from the mean. Or you think two identically shaped histograms at different locations have different SDs.

subtypes.name: Effect of changing data, and comparing centers across sets
subtypes.tell: The question asks what happens to the mean and/or median when a value is added (often an outlier), or which statement 'must be true' about two sets' means or medians. You may get box plots, frequency tables with symbolic values, or several tables to rank by mean. Roman-numeral I/II answer formats are common.
subtypes.method: 1) Adding an extreme value pulls the mean hard toward it but moves the median at most one position, so check whether the middle value actually changes. 2) Box plots show medians only, never means, so any mean claim is not 'must be true'. 3) For symmetric tables, the mean is the center of symmetry, so find the one that isn't symmetric and see which way it leans.
subtypes.desmos: Usually null: these are reasoning questions about how measures behave, often with symbolic or unspecified values. For numeric frequency tables you can check means with mean(values, frequencies).
subtypes.trap: You assume the median shifts as much as the mean when an outlier is added, or that it always changes. Or you infer something about the mean from a box plot. Or, with 'must be true' wording, you pick a claim that is merely possible.

subtypes.name: Find p% of a number
subtypes.tell: You get a total count or amount and one percent, and the question asks how many or how much that percent is. It may be written in words (tiles, seeds, seats, a tip on a bill) or as a bare 'what is p% of N'. Sometimes the percent is in a table and you first add two categories together. The answer is always smaller than the total when p is under 100.
subtypes.method: 1) Change the percent to a decimal by moving the point two places left. 2) Multiply it by the total. 3) If the question asks about 'either A or B' from a table, add the two percents before you multiply.
subtypes.desmos: Type the product straight in, for example 0.15*78.2, and read the value. You could do it by hand just as fast. The calculator only saves time when the decimals are awkward.
