subtypes.method: 1) Mark the old view and the evidence it rested on. 2) Check that the new data attacks that exact reasoning. 3) Choose the option that restates the old view, since that is what's being doubted, and not a new claim the study makes.
subtypes.trap: You pick something the new evidence supports, or a stronger claim the study never tested, when the blank wants the old idea being overturned. The wrong answers often mention the right topic but attach to the wrong side of the 'however'.

subtypes.name: The conclusion has to hedge
subtypes.tell: The passage describes a study or observation, then adds a complication: a variable nobody controlled, erosion or change since the event, a small or special sample. It ends 'the results therefore ___' or just 'Therefore, ___'. The right answer usually uses 'might not', 'could suggest ... even though' or 'may not accurately reflect'.
subtypes.method: 1) Name the flaw or confound in a few words. 2) Ask what that flaw makes uncertain, which is usually the link between what was measured and what it's supposed to show. 3) Choose the cautious option that says the evidence may be misleading, not the one that states a firm new fact.
subtypes.trap: You pick a confident conclusion, like 'X was smaller than thought' or 'the method proves Y'. But the complication only takes away certainty. It doesn't prove the opposite. Firm claims in either direction are wrong here.

subtypes.name: Predict the researchers' hypothesis
subtypes.tell: The passage lays out a puzzling observation: an odd trait, an unexpected location, a behaviour that doesn't seem to fit. Or it sets up an experiment and what the researchers expected. The blank follows 'the team hypothesizes that', 'anticipated that ... would' or 'suggesting that'.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the surprise, or the pattern the researchers expect to hold or reverse. 2) Ask what one explanation or outcome would make every stated detail make sense. If the setup says an effect will flip, flip it. 3) Choose the option that explains the puzzle using only the details the passage gives you.
subtypes.trap: You pick an explanation that sounds scientific but ignores a key detail, such as the setting, the comparison group or the direction of the effect. Or, in a flipped-effect setup, you choose the original effect instead of its reverse.

subtypes.name: What must this person believe?
subtypes.tell: The passage reports what one person or group did or said: a review, a search, a recommendation, a study they chose to run. The blank follows 'this suggests that in X's view', 'this approach suggests X thought' or 'X's recommendation implies that'. You're being asked about an unstated assumption, not a fact.
subtypes.method: 1) Ask why a reasonable person would take that exact action or make that exact statement. 2) Work out the belief the action depends on. If they recommend a new tool, they think the current one falls short. 3) Choose the option that states that assumption, and not one that contradicts it or reverses a comparison.
subtypes.trap: The wrong answers reverse a comparison, for example saying the earlier version was better, or they attribute a belief the person never needed. Some go too far, such as saying the old tool is useless when the person only thinks it's limited.

subtypes.name: Name the mismatch or unintended effect
subtypes.tell: The passage sets two things against each other: something seems simple but is demanding, a policy has a goal but also a loophole, one kind of work is easy to reach and another isn't. The blank follows 'there is a disparity between', 'the unintended effect of', 'those who ... risk' or 'Consequently'.
subtypes.method: 1) Put the two sides of the contrast into your own words. 2) Choose the option that names that exact pair, or that states what naturally follows from the gap. For an unintended effect, it's usually the opposite of the policy's goal. 3) Check that both halves of the option match the passage.
subtypes.trap: You pick a choice that pairs the wrong two things, or that states only one side of the contrast. For unintended-effect questions, you pick something that harms the side the policy already favours, when the answer is the harm to the side it was meant to protect.

subtypes.name: Zoom in on one named detail
subtypes.tell: The goal names one specific thing: a single work, one year, one feature, one aspect (for example 'describe the setting of X', 'describe how material is used in Y', 'accomplishments before event Z'). The notes cover several related things, and the answer choices are all accurate sentences drawn from different parts of the notes.
subtypes.method: 1) Underline the exact noun and restriction in the goal (which item, which time period, which feature). 2) Cross out any choice that is mainly about a different item or time, or about the general topic. 3) Pick the choice whose main clause directly gives that detail. The target has to be the subject of the sentence, not tucked into a side clause.
subtypes.trap: Every choice is true to the notes, so if you check for accuracy you'll keep all four. The trap choices mention the right name but describe the wrong thing, such as the author's biography instead of the novel's setting, or a later period when the goal says 'before'. Some cover the whole collection when the goal asks about one member of it.

subtypes.name: Emphasize a similarity
subtypes.tell: The goal says 'emphasize a similarity between' two items. The notes run in parallel blocks, one per item, and the blocks usually share one feature while differing on others. Some choices use contrast words like 'whereas', 'but', or 'unlike'.
subtypes.method: 1) Before you look at the choices, scan the two blocks and find the one attribute they share. 2) Pick the choice that states that shared attribute for both items, usually with 'both' or 'each' or a single predicate covering the pair. 3) Drop any choice built on a contrast word or one that describes only one item.
subtypes.trap: The notes contain more differences than similarities, so most choices accurately describe a difference, and they often sound more detailed and impressive. Another trap is a choice that gives one item's feature and never states that the other item has it too.

subtypes.name: Emphasize a difference / compare two things
subtypes.tell: The goal says 'emphasize a difference', 'contrast', or 'compare' two items (types, hypotheses, species, programs). Sometimes it is narrowed further, for example 'compare the disadvantages' or 'emphasize the significance of one date relative to another'. The notes give parallel facts for each item, often with numbers or opposite traits.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the attribute that the goal restricts you to (disadvantages, size, composition, scope), if it names one. 2) Pick the choice that names BOTH items and puts their different values on that same attribute side by side, usually with 'whereas', 'while', or 'but', or with a comparative. 3) Reject choices that just list both items or give only one item's value.
subtypes.trap: Some choices mention both items but never state how they differ ('two types include A and B'). Others give a contrast on the wrong attribute, such as an advantage when the goal asked for disadvantages. On narrowed goals, the trap is a choice that compares the items on some other feature instead of the one the goal specifies.

subtypes.name: Present a study's aim, method, or conclusion
subtypes.tell: The notes follow a research story: background or gap, who did the study, what they did, what they found, and what they concluded. The goal names ONE stage: 'emphasize the aim', 'present the conclusion', 'present the study and its findings', or a recommendation that came out of it.
subtypes.method: 1) Match the goal word to a stage: aim means purpose or question ('sought to', 'investigated whether'), findings or conclusion means result ('found', 'concluded', 'determined'), and a recommendation means advice. 2) Pick the choice built around that stage's content. For 'study and findings', the choice has to name the study AND its result.
subtypes.trap: Choices describe the wrong stage of the same study. When the goal asks for the aim, the trap reports the result. When it asks for the conclusion, the trap describes the method or the background debate. When the goal says 'study and its findings', the trap gives only one of the two.

subtypes.name: Emphasize significance / achievement
subtypes.tell: The goal uses a value word: 'emphasize the significance of', 'emphasize the achievement', 'historical significance'. The notes build to one note that says why the thing matters: something rare, transitional, first, successful, or earlier than others.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the note that explains why it matters, not the one that tells what or who. It usually comes near the end, or it is the note that sets the item against a background claim. 2) Pick the choice that states the outcome or importance, not just the event or the person. 3) If the significance is relative, such as 'earliest' or 'unlike others', make sure the choice includes the comparison that makes it significant.
subtypes.trap: The trap choices describe the thing accurately (who found it, what it looks like, when it happened) but never say why it matters. A related trap gives a bare date or fact that is significant only when compared with something else, and the choice leaves that comparison out.

subtypes.name: Generalization vs. specific example
subtypes.tell: The goal says 'make a generalization about' a category or 'provide an example of' something. The notes mix a category-level definition or statement with one or more specific instances.
subtypes.method: 1) Decide which level the goal wants. A generalization is a claim about the whole category with no single instance as its subject. An example is one named instance tied to the category. 2) For a generalization, pick the choice that makes a broad claim, often using 'most', 'all', or the plural category noun. For an example, pick the choice that names a specific item AND links it to the property in the goal, even if the notes use another name for that property.
subtypes.trap: The trap is the wrong level. For a generalization, the trap lists specific instances or compares two of them. For an example, the trap is a general category statement with no specific instance named. Example questions also often switch terminology, where the goal uses a synonym that appears in only one note, so a choice can seem to miss the property when it actually has it.

subtypes.name: Introduce to an unfamiliar audience
subtypes.tell: The goal says 'introduce X to a new audience', or it names an audience that isn't familiar with the topic. The notes include a basic definition of what X is, plus secondary facts such as founding dates, spin-offs, and later developments.
subtypes.method: 1) Ask what a reader who has never heard of X needs first: what it is and what it does. 2) Pick the choice that names X and gives its identifying description or purpose in one sentence. 3) Drop choices that assume the reader already knows what X is.
subtypes.trap: The trap choices sit on a secondary detail, such as an offshoot organization, a date, or one narrow aim, without ever saying what X is. They also treat X as already known, which works for an informed reader but fails the stated audience.

subtypes.name: Overall structure: match the two-part outline
subtypes.tell: The question asks which choice best describes the overall structure of the text, and every answer choice follows the pattern 'It does X, then does Y.' The passage is usually a short informational text of 3-5 sentences with one clear turn.
subtypes.method: 1) Write a 2-3 word label for the job of each sentence or chunk (introduces, explains, qualifies, challenges). 2) Find where the text turns, usually at 'However,' 'Still,' 'But,' or 'Thus.' 3) Check both halves of each choice against your labels. If either half is wrong, eliminate that choice.
subtypes.trap: Wrong choices usually get the first half right and the second half wrong. The second half either describes a move the text never makes (a proposed solution, a history, several examples when there is only one) or gets the direction of the turn wrong (supports instead of complicates). You pick a choice after reading only half of it.

subtypes.name: Set up a belief, then knock it down
subtypes.tell: The text starts with what 'many researchers assume,' 'people long thought,' or 'some studies suggest.' It then offers a finding or example that complicates that view. The question may ask about structure or main purpose. Correct choices use words like 'challenges,' 'complicates,' or 'cautions against overstating.'
subtypes.method: 1) Find the belief at the start and decide whether the author endorses or doubts it, using signals like 'however,' 'but,' 'we should not overstate,' or 'busted the myth.' 2) Treat the rest of the text as evidence for that doubt. 3) Pick the choice whose verb says 'questions' or 'challenges' and names the right belief, not the evidence.
subtypes.trap: Most of the text is about the study or example, so you pick 'to describe an experiment' or 'to present findings about X.' That is what the text contains, not what it is for. On the harder items, the other trap is a choice that claims the author rejects the idea entirely when the text only warns against overstating it.

subtypes.name: Function of the underlined sentence (science/history text)
subtypes.tell: The question asks for the function of the underlined sentence or portion 'in the text as a whole.' The passage is a science, research, or history text. The choices start with role verbs: 'It elaborates on,' 'It presents a finding,' 'It defines a term,' 'It summarizes the results,' 'It explains a method.'
subtypes.method: 1) Ignore what the underlined part says and ask what it does for the sentence before and after it: is it background, a claim, a method, a result, an example, or a definition? 2) Check that the choice names the right idea it connects to. 3) Eliminate choices whose verb is too strong (dismisses, refutes) or that point to the wrong part of the text.
subtypes.trap: A choice copies words from the underlined part but gives the wrong role, such as calling a result 'a method' or a researcher's finding 'the researcher's remarks.' Other choices have the relation wrong: 'dismisses the previous sentence' when the underlined part actually extends it. You go by matching words, not by the role.

subtypes.name: Function of the underlined line (fiction/memoir)
subtypes.tell: The passage is introduced with 'The following text is from [author's] [year] novel/memoir/story.' It is only 2-4 sentences long, and one line is underlined. The choices describe what that line accomplishes: contrasts two characters, illustrates a feeling, summarizes what came before, or describes an event.
subtypes.method: 1) Read the sentence right before and right after the underlined line, since its job is almost always defined by what sits next to it. 2) Say in plain words what the line shows, e.g. 'shows the character is different from X' or 'shows a thing means more than its literal use.' 3) Pick the choice that matches that, including any figurative meaning.
subtypes.trap: Choices take the line too literally, for example reading a symbolic image as a physical fact. Or they invent content the text never shows, such as a conversation, a dislike, or a list of topics. Before you pick a choice, check that you can point to the words that support it.

subtypes.name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work, or thing
subtypes.tell: The question asks for the main purpose or overall purpose of the text, and every choice starts with 'To...'. The passage introduces an artist, activist, organization, invention, or phenomenon and gives facts or examples about it. There is no clear counterargument in the text.
subtypes.method: 1) Ask what every sentence has in common, since the purpose has to cover the whole text and not just its opening or last line. 2) Match the choice's verb to the tone: 'describe,' 'illustrate,' or 'provide examples of' fits neutral exposition, while 'argue' or 'criticize' needs an explicit opinion in the text. 3) Eliminate any choice that covers only one detail or introduces a comparison the text doesn't make.
subtypes.trap: Several choices name a detail that really is in the text, like one achievement, the founder's motive, or a single example, but that is too narrow to be the purpose. Other choices use verbs that are too strong ('argue that X should be recognized') when the text only informs. You pick a true detail instead of the purpose of the whole text.

subtypes.name: Main purpose: what a study or mechanism shows
subtypes.tell: The text walks through a method, experiment, or process (researchers did A, measured B, found C, or 'when X happens, Y happens'). The question asks for the main purpose, and choices mix 'to describe an experiment that...' or 'to explain how X works' with comparisons or evaluations.
subtypes.method: 1) Decide whether the text only reports (describe or explain) or also evaluates (criticize, question). 2) Check what the choice claims about the result: does it say the study answered a question, raised a new one, or supported a hypothesis? Confirm that against the last sentence. 3) For process texts, pick the choice that names the whole mechanism, not one step or a comparison.
subtypes.trap: A choice correctly says 'describes an experiment' but misstates the result, for example saying the question went unresolved when the text gives clear results. Or a choice claims the text compares two things when only one is explained. Read the whole choice, not just its opening verb.

subtypes.name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
subtypes.tell: The passage is introduced with 'The following text is from/adapted from [author's] [year] novel/poem/story/memoir,' often with a bracketed setup sentence. The question asks for the main purpose, and the choices start with 'To portray...,' 'To convey...,' 'To encourage...,' or 'To give an example of...'.
subtypes.method: 1) Use the setup line to identify who the focus is (the narrator, a named character, or the addressee of the poem). 2) Say in plain words what the excerpt as a whole shows about that person, such as their reaction, a trait, a hope, or a feeling of being torn. 3) Pick the choice that names the right person and the right emotion or trait. Watch the tone: encouraging is not the same as warning.
subtypes.trap: Choices mention the right characters but shift the focus to the wrong person, for example the father's pride instead of the boy's wish. Or they name a concrete detail the text never gives, like which topics were discussed or how the friends met. In poems, a choice may reverse the tone, turning an encouraging poem into a warning or a lament. Stick to what the excerpt as a whole conveys.

subtypes.name: Two things set side by side (By contrast / Conversely)
subtypes.tell: You see two parallel categories, groups or cases described with the same sentence frame, where one attribute flips: above/below, one/many, follows the rule/breaks the rule. Often the blank sits mid-sentence after the second subject, set off by commas. The choices mix one contrast word with example, sequence and conclusion words.
subtypes.method: 1) Name the subject of each sentence and the attribute given for each. 2) If the subjects differ and the attributes are opposites, pick the comparison-contrast word (by contrast, conversely, in comparison only if it's framed as a difference). 3) Rule out 'similarly' and 'likewise', which need the same attribute.
subtypes.trap: In the harder versions, sentence one states a general tendency and the blank sentence brings in one specific case. You reach for 'for example' because a specific item follows. But that case goes against the tendency, so it's a contrast, not an illustration. Before you call something an example, check that the specific case actually agrees with the general claim.

subtypes.name: Expectation, then surprise (However / Nonetheless / That said / Actually)
subtypes.tell: Sentence one sets up a belief, assumption, appearance or hope: 'may seem', 'many assume', 'have long believed', or a list of big achievements. The blank sentence reports the reality that undercuts it, such as a failure, a correction or an unexpected exception. Choices include one concession or correction word and several continuation words.
subtypes.method: 1) Ask whether sentence two is what sentence one would lead you to expect. 2) If it isn't, you need a concession: however, nonetheless, that said, still. If sentence one is a mistaken belief and sentence two gives the true fact, 'actually' or 'in fact' fits best. 3) Check that the choice doesn't also claim a cause, which would be wrong here.
subtypes.trap: Two traps here. First, you pick 'for this reason' or 'moreover' because both sentences are about the same topic and you never check the direction of the logic. Second, you rule out 'however' when sentence one is a string of successes, because you don't notice that sentence two ranks one success above all the others and so pivots against the list.

subtypes.name: Result of what came before (Thus / Hence / For this reason / As such)
subtypes.tell: The earlier sentences give a constraint, need, principle or piece of evidence. The blank sentence describes an action someone took, an outcome or a conclusion that happens because of it. You can put 'so' between the sentences and it reads naturally. Choices mix one cause-effect word with contrast, example and time words.
subtypes.method: 1) Put 'so' or 'because of that' in the blank and read it aloud. 2) If it holds, pick the choice that means therefore: thus, hence, for this reason, consequently, as such. 3) If more than one cause word appears, use the one whose tone fits. 'As such' works when sentence two classifies what sentence one described.
subtypes.trap: You mix up 'an example of the principle' with 'the result of applying the principle'. When sentence one states a general rule and sentence two shows someone using that rule to reach a finding, 'for example' looks right. But the finding follows from the rule, so a cause-effect word is correct. Also watch for decoys like 'consequently' when sentence two just corrects sentence one and doesn't follow from it.

subtypes.name: General claim, then the detail (For example vs Specifically / In particular)
subtypes.tell: Sentence one makes a broad claim: 'several roles', 'improved upon', 'has also done', 'underwent a transformation', 'many authors'. The blank sentence zooms in. Choices often include both 'for example' and 'specifically' or 'in particular', or one of them next to contrast and sequence decoys.
subtypes.method: 1) Confirm that sentence two is narrower than sentence one and agrees with it. 2) Decide whether it's one instance out of several possible ones ('for example') or an exact spelling-out of the same claim ('specifically', 'in particular'). If sentence one mentions a single vague thing and sentence two says exactly what it was, pick 'specifically'. If sentence one mentions a class or a plural and sentence two picks one member, pick 'for example'. 3) Eliminate anything that implies contrast or time order.
subtypes.trap: You choose 'for example' when sentence one names one single event or action and sentence two just restates it in detail. Nothing is being chosen from a set, so 'specifically' is the answer. The reverse mistake also happens: you pick 'in other words' when sentence two adds new, narrower information and doesn't simply rephrase.

subtypes.name: Adding another point, or doubling down (In addition / Moreover / Indeed)
subtypes.tell: Sentence two points the same way as sentence one. Either it's a second, separate item of the same kind (another achievement, another use, another function), or it's the same claim restated more strongly or backed up with vivid support. Choices include 'additionally', 'in addition', 'moreover' or 'indeed' next to contrast and cause decoys.
subtypes.method: 1) Check that sentence two agrees with sentence one and doesn't turn against it. 2) If it's a new, parallel item, pick an addition word: additionally, in addition, moreover. If it strengthens, confirms or vividly elaborates the same point, pick 'indeed' or 'in fact'. 3) Make sure it isn't narrower (that would be example or specification) and isn't caused by sentence one.
subtypes.trap: 'Indeed' feels wrong to you when sentence two seems to contrast with the words just before it. In fact it supports the larger claim, for example by showing why something counts as an outlier. You grab 'nevertheless' because of a surface contrast and miss that sentence two confirms the main point. You also confuse 'moreover', which adds a new point, with 'indeed', which reinforces the same one.

subtypes.name: Timeline and steps (Earlier / Previously / Later / Eventually)
subtypes.tell: The sentences carry dates, years, or process steps like 'first... then...'. The blank sentence moves to a different point in time. Most of the choices are time words that point in opposite directions (earlier or later, soon or eventually), plus one or two logic decoys.
subtypes.method: 1) Write down the time of each sentence: a year, 'step 1, step 2', or before/after. 2) Decide whether the blank sentence jumps backward (earlier, previously), forward (later, subsequently), or to the last step of a process (eventually, finally). 3) Pick the time word that matches that direction.
subtypes.trap: You assume the text runs forward and pick 'next' or 'later' when the blank sentence actually goes back to an earlier date to give background. Compare the dates themselves, not the order of the sentences. You also pick a cause word ('as a result') just because one event came after another.

subtypes.name: The logical upshot (Ultimately / Then / In the end)
subtypes.tell: This is usually the hardest tier. The passage is abstract and dense, often about literature or the history of ideas. The blank may sit mid-sentence, e.g. 'It may not have been..., ______, that...'. Sentence two is a summary judgment or an inference drawn from the setup, not a single effect. Choices are several words that all sound plausible for adding or concluding: to that end, moreover, hence, then, ultimately.
subtypes.method: 1) Decide whether sentence two is a final judgment that brings together tensions described earlier ('ultimately', 'in the end') or a reasonable inference that follows from the premise ('then', in the sense of 'it follows that'). 2) Test each decoy strictly: 'to that end' needs a stated goal, 'hence' needs a direct cause, and 'moreover' needs a separate new point. 3) Keep the choice whose precise requirement the passage actually meets.
subtypes.trap: The decoys are near-synonyms, and each has a narrow condition you forget to check. 'To that end' introduces how a purpose is carried out, not a conclusion. 'Hence' needs a mechanical cause-effect link. 'Moreover' adds a new point. You pick whichever one 'sounds academic' instead of testing its exact logical job.

subtypes.name: “Most nearly mean” in a literary excerpt
subtypes.tell: You see no blank. The prompt names a word or short phrase in quotation marks and asks what it most nearly means as used in the text. The passage is usually an adapted poem or older prose, often with an introduction naming the author and date. The choices are single words or short phrases that could all be dictionary meanings of the word.
subtypes.method: 1) Cover the choices, reread the line that contains the word, and put in a plain word of your own that fits the image or comparison around it. 2) Pick the choice that matches your word, then put it back into the line to confirm it keeps the meaning of the sentence.
subtypes.trap: You pick the word's most common meaning, or a meaning suggested by how it looks or sounds, when the poem is using a different or figurative sense. Another trap is a choice that fits the poem's overall mood but does not mean the same as the word.

subtypes.name: Blank defined by the next sentence or after a colon
subtypes.tell: A blank sits in one sentence, and the next sentence begins with an example marker (such as 'for example') or follows a colon or dash. That second part describes concretely what the blank means. The blank is usually a noun or adjective that sums up that description.
subtypes.method: 1) Skip the blank and read the explanation or example that follows it. 2) Write down a one-word summary of what it shows. 3) Choose the option that matches your summary most exactly, not just in general tone.
subtypes.trap: You choose a word that is on topic, or that suits the subject in general, but does not name what the example actually shows. For instance, you pick a positive word when the evidence points to one specific quality, such as precision.

subtypes.name: Contrast pivot (but / while / however / instead)
subtypes.tell: You see a contrast word such as 'but', 'while', 'although', 'however', 'instead', 'despite' or 'counterintuitive'. The blank sits on one side of the contrast, and the other side has a clear positive or negative charge, or a clear situation.
subtypes.method: 1) Find the contrast word and work out what the other side says. 2) Your blank must mean roughly the opposite of that side, so predict that opposite. 3) Check the choices for the correct direction first, then for the precise meaning.
subtypes.trap: You pick a word that repeats the other side of the contrast because it sounds related, or you miss that 'counterintuitive' means the result goes against what you would expect.

subtypes.name: Cause-and-effect logic (because / since / so / led to)
subtypes.tell: The blank sits inside a reason clause or a result clause, marked by words such as 'because', 'since', 'for this reason', 'so', 'thus', or a phrase saying one thing led to another. The choices are often verbs of change (increase, reduce, cause, block) or adjectives that describe a process.
subtypes.method: 1) State the chain in plain words: X happens, so Y. 2) Ask which word has to fill the blank for the chain to make sense physically or logically. 3) Eliminate choices that reverse the direction or describe a different kind of effect.
subtypes.trap: You pick a verb that goes in the right general direction but acts on the wrong thing, such as 'hides' when the text needs 'reduces'. You can also get the direction backwards because the causal chain has two steps.

subtypes.name: Hidden negative that flips the polarity
subtypes.tell: Around the blank you see a word that reverses meaning: 'less', 'lacked', 'unlikely to be', 'little more than', 'challenging the view that', 'preclude', 'disproves'. The wording makes you work out the opposite of what the evidence shows.
subtypes.method: 1) Say what the evidence says is actually true. 2) Apply the reversal: if the text denies the blank or challenges it, the blank is the opposite of the evidence. 3) Put your choice back in and read the whole sentence, including the negative, to check it.
subtypes.trap: You match the blank to the evidence directly and skip the reversal. You end up with the exact opposite of the answer, and that opposite is always one of the choices.

subtypes.name: How findings relate to a claim (support / undermine / question)
subtypes.tell: The text sets up a belief, hypothesis or skepticism, then brings in researchers, data or a study, and the blank is the verb or noun that links the new evidence to the earlier view. The choices are verbs of reasoning or attitude, such as assume, question, confirm, reveal, anticipate or regret.
subtypes.method: 1) Decide whether the new evidence agrees with the earlier view or goes against it. 2) Decide whether the blank describes the evidence or the people who held the view. 3) Pick the choice with that exact relationship, for example confirming rather than merely showing.
subtypes.trap: You choose a neutral 'research-sounding' verb such as reveal or inspect that doesn't express agreement or disagreement. Or you mix up who is doing what, for example you pick 'questioned' for people who actually held the assumption.

subtypes.name: Word + preposition choices (attitude or ability toward something)
subtypes.tell: Each choice is a short phrase ending in a preposition, such as 'X to', 'X with', 'X by', 'X for' or 'X in'. The blank describes a person's or group's attitude, experience, or reaction toward something named right after it.
subtypes.method: 1) Use the rest of the text to decide whether the relationship is positive or negative, and whether it describes skill, feeling, or openness. 2) Read each phrase in place as a whole unit, and keep the one whose meaning matches your prediction and whose preposition fits naturally.
subtypes.trap: You are drawn to a strong, vivid phrase such as 'angered by' or 'excited about' that fits the topic, when the logic calls for a milder or different relationship, such as openness or lack of experience.

subtypes.name: Advanced-vocabulary choices with close meanings
subtypes.tell: It is a Hard-level blank, and the choices are unusual or academic words, sometimes with an article attached ('a/an ___'). Several choices share a general tone, positive or negative, so the tone of the sentence alone won't settle it.
subtypes.method: 1) Work out a precise meaning for the blank from the logic of the sentence, not just its tone. 2) Cross out the choices you know don't fit. 3) Between the ones left, choose the word whose exact meaning fits, even if it's the one you know less well. Don't eliminate an unfamiliar word just because it's unfamiliar.
subtypes.trap: You pick the word you recognize because it roughly fits, when the answer is an unfamiliar word that fits exactly. Or you get caught by a word that looks or sounds like the idea you want but means something unrelated.
